items.item: Minimal HUD with clear information hierarchy (critical vs on-demand)
Touch targets sized for thumbs, placed away from default jump/thumbstick, safe areas/notches
Controller navigation of inventory (selection/focus, back closes)
Responsive layout approach (scale, aspect ratio constraints, UIScale) rather than pixel-absolute
Server does not trust UI/inventory state from client

incorrect_or_stale: Uses 'sp' as a text-size unit. That is an Android unit; Roblox uses pixels or TextScaled.
The initial InputProfile resolution never detects Gamepad at startup, so a controller isn't recognised until the next input.
Advises using UIListLayout and UIGridLayout 'sparingly in hot paths'. This advice is dubious, because layout objects are the normal and efficient approach.
slop: Compass, quest tracker and time/temp widgets are added without justification for this game.
Generic feedback list: damage vignette, toast stack, slot flashes.
Says to 'test for colour-blindness' without saying how.
overengineering: User-draggable and resizable mobile action buttons as a baseline feature.

slop: A stray '*Apex: ui-ux → genres*' header artifact.
Diegetic heartbeat and breathing cues and directional damage indicators are offered as genre defaults.
overengineering: Crafting tab with pinned recipes, container Take All and death-drop UX, all beyond a HUD and inventory scope.
Optimistic client prediction with server reconciliation for inventory moves.
Three-tier layout classes on top of input profiles, with no concrete UIScale or aspect-ratio mechanism given.

raw.reason: B covers more rubric items in concrete terms: explicit back-to-close and NextSelection grid navigation, detailed server-side intent validation, and the inventory not pausing in a survival game. A is solid but leaves controller back handling and server authority vague.
